answer: Net billing in Pakistan charges every imported unit at your normal slab rate and credits each exported unit at a flat buyback rate, {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}} (NEPRA's national average energy purchase price). Net bill = imports × slab rate − exports × buyback rate: importing {{in.import_units|int}} and exporting {{in.export_units|int}} units costs {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}, against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} under old net metering.
how: Import: {{out.import_calc}} = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}. Export credit: {{out.export_units}} units × {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} = {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}. Net billing energy charge = {{out.import_energy_rs|rs}} − {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} = {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} (credit carried forward: {{out.carry_forward_rs|rs}}). Old net metering: {{out.nm_calc}} = {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Net billing costs {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more. Fixed charges, surcharges, adjustments and GST come on top of both.
key_facts: Pakistan replaced net metering with net billing for new solar connections under the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}: imported units are billed at the normal slab rate and exported units are credited at a separate buyback rate.

The buyback rate is the national average energy purchase price, {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit in NEPRA's decision for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}, far below the {{out.import_rate|rs2}} slab rate of a {{out.import_units|int}} unit month.

For a month with {{out.import_units|int}} units imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported, net billing charges {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} in energy against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}} under old net metering, {{out.extra_vs_net_metering_rs|rs}} more.
Under net billing the solar system you may connect may not exceed your sanctioned load, so the sanctioned load on the bill sets the largest system you can apply for.

Agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing.

formula.text: Net billing Rs = max(0, imported units × slab rate − exported units × buyback rate); old net metering Rs = max(0, imported − exported) × slab rate of the net units
lines: slab rate = A-1 domestic rate of the band the imported units reach (unprotected or protected)
buyback rate = flat Rs per exported unit; NEPRA's national average energy purchase price, editable in case NEPRA revises it
a credit larger than the import bill carries forward in rupees; the bill is never negative
energy charges only: fixed charge, FC surcharge, QTA, FPA and GST are added on the real bill

p: Until 2026 a home solar system in Pakistan was connected under net metering: a bidirectional meter counted units in and units out, and the DISCO billed only the difference. The {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, moved new connections to net billing. The meter is the same kind, but the two readings are now priced separately: imports at the normal tariff, exports at a buyback rate.

The change matters because the two prices are far apart. Under net metering an exported unit was worth as much as an imported one; under net billing it is worth the buyback rate, a fraction of the slab rate. Using your own solar power during the day is now worth much more than sending it to the grid.

sections.h2: Net billing vs net metering in Pakistan: a worked month
p: Take a month with {{out.import_units|int}} units imported and {{out.export_units|int}} exported. Net metering would bill {{out.net_metering_units|int}} net units at {{out.net_metering_rate|rs2}}, which is {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}. Net billing bills all {{out.import_units|int}} imported units at {{out.import_rate|rs2}} ({{out.import_energy_rs|rs}}) and credits {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} for the exports, leaving {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}}.

The gap comes from two places: the low buyback rate, and the slab. Under net metering the net units could fall into a cheaper band; under net billing the imported units alone set the band. A home that exports more than it imports still pays something under net billing, as the second example below shows.

sections.h2: NEPRA net billing buyback rate: where it comes from
p: The {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, do not print a rupee figure. They say exported units are credited at the national average energy purchase price, and NEPRA's decision on the power purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}} puts that price at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit. Both documents are listed under Sources. Some news reports gave other figures; these two NEPRA documents are the primary source.

Do not confuse it with the national average power purchase price, which also covers capacity payments and is not the export rate for new connections; agreements signed under the old regulations keep their old rate and billing method instead. NEPRA sets the energy purchase price again each year and may revise it by notification; if your bill shows another rate, enter it in the buyback field; the table below shows how much the monthly bill moves for each rupee of buyback.

sections.h2: Sanctioned load cap: how big can a net billing system be?
p: Under the new rules the solar system you may connect may not exceed your sanctioned load: the kW printed as sanctioned load on your bill is the largest solar system you could connect. If you want a larger system you have to apply for a higher sanctioned load first, which raises the fixed charge every month and, at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more, moves the connection to a time-of-use meter.

Size the connection with the [[N4|sanctioned load calculator]] before you size the panels, and confirm with your DISCO: the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, set the cap, and NEPRA may revise it by notification.

sections.h2: Is net metering ending in Pakistan? Existing contracts
p: For new applications, yes: they are processed under net billing. For homes already on net metering, NEPRA's amendment keeps agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} on the rate and rules of the old regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; a renewal is on net billing. Ask your DISCO when your agreement ends.

sections.h2: Net metering application: the steps in general
p: The steps are broadly the same under net billing as they were under net metering, but the forms and documents differ between DISCOs, so confirm each step with yours. First, check the sanctioned load on your bill and size the system within it. Second, choose an AEDB-certified installer: a vendor on the certified list of the Alternative Energy Development Board (AEDB), which the net-metering rules required and DISCOs still ask for; confirm with yours.

Third, the installer or you submit the application to the DISCO with the system details, the latest bill and identity documents. Fourth, the DISCO checks the connection and approves it, and an agreement is signed. Fifth, the DISCO installs the bidirectional meter and the system starts exporting. Do not switch on export before the meter is installed.

sections.h2: What net billing means for solar payback
p: Payback now depends mostly on how much of the solar output you use yourself. Every unit used at home saves the full slab rate of {{out.import_rate|rs2}}; every unit exported earns the buyback rate. Run the pump, washing machine, iron and AC in the day, and size the system to your daytime use rather than to the roof.
To estimate payback, take the system price from the solar price pages and divide it by the yearly saving: the bill you would pay without solar minus the net billing bill, over twelve months.

mistakes: Taking the buyback rate as fixed for years. NEPRA sets the energy purchase price again each year; check the rate on your bill each January.
Assuming an existing net-metering agreement is safe forever. It keeps the old terms only until it expires, and adding panels ends them sooner; check the end date with your DISCO.
Sizing the system to the roof instead of to the sanctioned load and daytime use. Under net billing the system may not exceed the sanctioned load, and exported units earn little.
Reading the result as the full bill. It is the energy charge only; fixed charges, surcharges, adjustments and GST are added on the real bill.
safety: Only a AEDB-certified installer and a licensed electrician may connect a solar system for export, and only the DISCO installs the bidirectional meter; never back-feed the grid through a socket or bypass the meter.

faq.q: What is net billing in Pakistan?
faq.a: A way of billing solar homes in which imported units are charged at the normal slab rate and exported units are credited at a lower buyback rate, {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}. It replaced net metering for new connections under the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}.

faq.q: What is the difference between net billing and net metering?
faq.a: Net metering subtracted exported units from imported units and billed the difference. Net billing prices them separately: imports at the slab rate, exports at the buyback rate. For {{out.import_units|int}} units in and {{out.export_units|int}} out that is {{out.net_energy_rs|rs}} against {{out.net_metering_rs|rs}}.

faq.q: What is the NEPRA net billing buyback rate?
faq.a: {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} per unit for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}. The regulations credit exports at the national average energy purchase price, and NEPRA's power purchase price decision puts it at that figure. NEPRA may revise it, so check your bill.

faq.q: Is net metering ending in Pakistan?
faq.a: For new connections, yes: they get net billing. Agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} keep the rate and rules of the old net-metering regulations until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing; renewals move to net billing.

faq.q: How big a solar system can I connect under net billing?
faq.a: Up to your sanctioned load under the regulations, so the sanctioned kW on your bill is the largest system you could connect. A higher sanctioned load raises the fixed charge and, at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more, means a time-of-use meter.

faq.q: How do I apply for net billing?
faq.a: Through your DISCO, usually via the installer: size the system within your sanctioned load, apply with the system details, latest bill and identity documents, wait for the DISCO's approval and agreement, then the DISCO fits a bidirectional meter. Documents vary by DISCO.

faq.q: Is solar still worth it under net billing?
faq.a: Usually yes, if most of the output is used at home in the day: each self-used unit saves the full slab rate of {{out.import_rate|rs2}}, while an exported unit earns only the buyback rate. Size the system to daytime use.
